title: My England Travelogue, Part 1, Ark Soane Academy
author: Doug Lemov
summary: Doug Lemov recounts a visit to Ark Soane Academy in Acton, hosted by Pritesh Raichura, describing the school as orderly, positive, and intentional about teaching. The centrepiece of the post is his account of Raichura's 'three phases of questioning' model: an opening phase of choral, low-stakes questions designed to maximise participation and pace from the first minute; a 'rehearsal and thinking' phase using rapid turn-and-talks to build memory through repetition rather than new content; and a checking-for-understanding phase, often using mini-whiteboards. Lemov notes the school's training materials explicitly warn teachers about pitfalls specific to each phase, reflecting a culture of careful self-study. He closes by musing he might adopt and adapt the model himself, possibly splitting rehearsal and thinking questions into separate phases.
points: Ark Soane's model breaks lesson questioning into three phases: participation/pace-building choral questions, rehearsal-and-thinking turn-and-talks aimed purely at building memory through repetition, and checking-for-understanding questions often via mini-whiteboards.

Lemov highlights that the school's own training materials name specific pitfalls for each phase -- for rehearsal-and-thinking, 'excessive parroting and little thinking' or 'rehearsing the wrong things' -- reflecting deliberate, evidence-grounded refinement.

He notes a key insight -- 'we are so apt to overlook memory' -- and calls the idea of asking questions merely to cause occasional rehearsal of key points the single most interesting and adoptable idea from the visit.
He proposes a refinement of his own: making the purpose of rehearsal questions explicit to students, since otherwise obviously-answered questions can feel demeaning without context.
quotes: The purposes of this sort of exchange are participation, accountability and pace. The teacher is reminding students that they will be active and busy throughout the lesson, and doing so right away.

A second phase of questioning was focused on rehearsal and thinking but the number of questions I saw that were simply about rehearsal was interesting - in many ways the most interesting idea that teaching at Ark Soane proposed.

For phase two questions (rehearsal and thinking), for example, teachers were warned to be careful of 'excessive parroting and little thinking'; 'rehearsing the wrong things—not the core knowledge; not making the most important links'.
We (people? educators?) are so apt to overlook memory. We assume remembering will happen on its own even though it doesn’t.
It’s probably the single idea I’d be most interested to borrow and adapt from my visit.
